newsitem.title: UK: British scientist develops first thinking machine.
newsitem.headline: British scientist develops first thinking machine.

text.p: A British professor said on Tuesday he had created the first machine able to think for itself and said it could help unlock some of the secrets of the human brain.

Professor Igor Aleksander of London's Imperial College of Science, Technology and Medicine used computer software to demonstrate how his creation, Magnus, could gather information and make rudimentary decisions.
Magnus could help researchers to understand how the brain absorbs and processes information and what consciousness means, Aleksander told a lecture at London's Science Museum.

The brain is the least understood part of the human body. Scientists know that neurons, or brain cells, exchange information and send signals around the body, but understand little about how these work.
Magnus could help explain just this, Aleksander said.
The machine, made up of artificial neurons, was shown a series of pictures -- a cat, a mouse and a butterfly -- and was able to recreate and recognise these.

Magnus also learned the sequence of the pictures and was later shown to have memorised where different images were placed on a "map" on the screen and to make arbitrary decisions about routes it took around the map.
When the machine was put to "sleep" it recalled images it had been shown in an earlier experiment.
"This is familiar in humans, the bringing up of unconsciousness through sleep," said Aleksander. "The images were only accessible when asleep since they had been learned in the previous world."

According to Aleksander, the brain may absorb information about the world around it and develop responses in the same way as Magnus does. He said Magnus was about one millionth as powerful as the human brain.
A baby is born with the ability to move its limbs, but until its brain's cognitive functions have developed, those movements are disordered and aimless.
Memory and experience are vital to its ability to make decisions and use its body in a deliberate and useful way.
"Memory forms a major feature of consciousness," said Aleksander, "...(it) may be involved in the perception of the present and a prediction of the future."
He was dismissive of fears that he may have created the first of a breed of thinking machines that in science fiction would end up ruling the world.
"There is no need to fear the conscious machine of the future. It will be friendly, easy to use and a joy to know."
But other scientists doubted he had invented a truly intelligent machine.
"I don't think anyone would realistically think that what Professor Aleksander has created is anything like consciousness," said Steven Rose of Britain's Open University.
"Definitions of consciousness without the experience, history and social relations which shape human consciousness would seem to be very lacking indeed."
